source.title: Towards Interpretable Protein Structure Prediction with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Nithin Parsan; David Yang; John J. Yang

record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse autoencoders to protein language models and measures how well their learned features align with biological concepts; this is an extension to a new model domain, not a test of the original toy-network geometry.
record.gate_note: Only the Swiss-Prot feature-to-concept results are rows for V4. The structure-prediction and contact-map results assess downstream preservation, not whether SAE features recover biological concepts. The steering results are induced interventions and do not measure naturally occurring feature organization. Cited results from other papers are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on a new kind of model (ESM2 protein language models, 8M and 3B). It measures how many Swiss-Prot biological concepts SAE features recover at F1 > 0.5. That bears on V4's claim that real models contain sparse features a dictionary can recover. The test is weak: there is no neuron or random-feature baseline, so the study cannot show that the concepts are superposed rather than neuron-aligned.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add the following. The authors conclude that SAEs scale to ESM2-3B and that Matryoshka SAEs match or beat TopK and L1. The 3B SAEs outperform 8M SAEs on concept discovery and contact prediction. The SAE reconstructions preserve ESMFold structure prediction. A single feature can steer predicted solvent accessibility.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse autoencoders and Swiss-Prot concept alignment in protein language models; it does not reproduce Toy Models of Superposition's toy-network setup or geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Model scale changes concept-discovery performance; at 8M, TopK identifies more concepts above F1 > 0.5 than Matryoshka, while the 3B variants identify the same total.
record.problems: Concept alignment is evaluated against a particular Swiss-Prot annotation procedure and threshold; the paper notes SAE features may vary with initialization and the UniRef50 sample. Only 8M and 3B model scales are evaluated.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results left out; downstream RMSD, contact-map, and induced steering results were omitted because they do not measure V4's feature-to-concept recovery.

untested.parts: No toy models, geometry, or sparsity-dependent phase transitions.
No test of capacity competition or of dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of alternative causes of polysemanticity.
No comparison of SAE features against individual neurons; the superposition-over-neurons result is only cited from InterPLM. No general-purpose text LLMs.
Completeness, stability and canonicity are not measured. The authors only note sensitivity to initialization, citing Paulo and Belrose.
No test of whether features are one-dimensional.

missing.what: Distribution of best F1 per concept: 3B medians are around 0.4, 8M medians are below 0.1.
Within-scale architecture differences are minimal (average F1 difference < 0.01). Relevant to whether recovery depends on SAE choice.

record.verdict_notes: The link to V4 is indirect. The study shows that SAE features align with annotated concepts in protein LMs, but it gives no neuron or random-direction baseline, so it does not by itself show superposition. Steering, RMSD and contact-map results are correctly excluded from the rows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy-network superposition, its geometric arrangement, or sparsity-dependent transitions.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise from limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
Tests SAE recovery of biological concepts in protein language models using Swiss-Prot annotations. Does not measure feature spreading across neurons or test general-purpose LLMs.
Does not test SAE feature completeness, stability across training runs, or canonical status.
Does not test whether model features are intrinsically one-dimensional directions.
